summary: Describes a standard way to encode email containing Greek text and gives guidance for implementers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Early email did not know the Greek alphabet. This explains how to write Greek letters so they arrive correctly in a message.

questions: how to send greek text in email
base64 vs quoted-printable for greek text
subtitle: How to send email with Greek text and ensure it arrives correctly.

tldr.problem: Email systems historically used ASCII and Latin characters. Sending Greek text required encoding it in a way both the sender and receiver could reliably handle.
tldr.mechanism: Greek text must be converted to the ISO 8859-7 character set, then encoded using either Base64 (preferred for mostly Greek text) or Quoted-Printable (when Greek is mixed with Latin), as defined in MIME.
tldr.outcome: Users can send and receive email with Greek characters reliably by following a standard encoding based on MIME and ISO 8859-7, though not all systems implement it correctly.

today: RFC 1947 remains the standard for Greek email. Modern email clients handle ISO 8859-7 and other character sets transparently, so users rarely need to think about encoding. However, the RFC remains a reference for implementers and for systems in regions with limited email infrastructure that still rely on explicit encoding.

sections.title: The Problem of Greek Text in Email
sections.content:
Email systems were designed for ASCII (7-bit characters), primarily Latin letters. When users wanted to send Greek text, they faced a problem: the mail system did not preserve it. Different systems used different encoding schemes, and messages often arrived garbled or unreadable.

RFC 822 defines the format of email messages; RFC 1521 defines MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions), which allows messages to carry any character set and specifies how to encode them. This RFC applies those standards specifically to Greek text, recommending ISO 8859-7 (a Latin-Greek character set standard) as the character encoding and either Base64 or Quoted-Printable as the transport encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: When you want to send a message in Greek, the computer needs to turn the Greek letters into numbers, send those numbers through the email system, and then the receiver's computer has to turn them back into Greek letters.

sections.title: Encoding Greek Text with MIME
sections.content:
To send Greek text, convert the text to the ISO 8859-7 character set. Then encode the result using either Base64 (recommended for text that is mostly Greek) or Quoted-Printable (when Greek text is interspersed with Latin).

Base64 expands the text by 33% but is always reliable. Quoted-Printable keeps ASCII characters as-is and encodes only special characters, so a message with mostly English and a few Greek words stays readable in the email.

The email must include MIME headers: MIME-Version: 1.0, Content-Type: text/plain; charset=ISO-8859-7, and Content-Transfer-Encoding: BASE64 (or Quoted-Printable). These headers tell the receiver's mail client how to decode the message.
sections.plainLanguage: You pick either Base64 (encode everything, always safe) or Quoted-Printable (keep English words readable, encode only the Greek), then label the message with headers that say how it is encoded.

sections.title: Character Set Mappings
sections.content:
The RFC includes a comprehensive table mapping every Greek character (from Unicode point U+0386 onwards) to its representation in ISO 8859-7 and in many other encoding schemes (PC code pages, Microsoft Windows, Apple Macintosh, and various ISO standards). This table enables conversion between different systems.

For example, Greek capital alpha (Α, Unicode U+0391) is 0xc1 in ISO 8859-7 and 0x41 in various other schemes. Small alpha (α, U+03b1) is 0xe1 in ISO 8859-7. The table helps implementers avoid creating garbled text when converting between character sets.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a big table that says which number represents each Greek letter in each system. You look up your Greek letter and find the number that matches your system.

sections.title: Common Implementation Errors
sections.content:
The RFC highlights mistakes commonly made when handling Greek email. One error is to set up a mail user agent with an ISO 8859-1 (Latin) font but using a keyboard and display font that shows Greek glyphs. The resulting message headers claim ISO 8859-1 but the body contains Greek text in a completely different encoding. This works between similar systems by accident but breaks everywhere else.

Another common mistake is to tag Microsoft Windows Greek text as ISO 8859-7 without converting it. The Microsoft Windows Greek character set differs from ISO 8859-7 in several code points. Converting without translation causes characters to display incorrectly.

A third error is to assume that early Microsoft Windows code pages match ISO 8859-7, when they actually differ (for historical reasons related to Windows glyph design). Correct handling requires an explicit translation step.
sections.plainLanguage: Many people make shortcuts: using a Greek font but lying about the encoding, or assuming Windows Greek is the same as the standard, or just mixing formats. These work sometimes by accident, but they break a lot of other things.

sections.title: Optional Header Encoding
sections.content:
It is recommended (though not required) to also encode Greek text that appears in email headers—the From, To, Subject, and other header fields. RFC 1522 specifies a method for this. The B-encoding format (Base64) is the default for encoding full Greek words in headers. The Q-encoding format (Quoted-Printable) is used when encoding just a single Greek character or word within a mainly Latin header.

When all email systems implement 8-bit transparency (a future state described in RFC 1425 and RFC 1426), header encoding may become unnecessary. Until then, this mechanism ensures headers remain readable.
sections.plainLanguage: If you put Greek in the Subject line or From field, you can encode it the same way. Use Base64 for a whole Greek word, or Quoted-Printable if it is just one letter in English.
